notes: Premade programme library for AJ Training. User-facing text is British English with no effort jargon.

glossary.To failure: The last rep you can complete with full range and control. If you tried another, it would not go up.
glossary.To technical failure: The last rep you can do with perfect form. Used on barbell lifts where grinding ugly reps is risky.
glossary.Drop set: At failure, immediately reduce the weight by about 25% and go to failure again.
glossary.Myo-reps: At failure, rest 5 slow breaths, do 3 to 5 more reps, repeat about 3 times.
glossary.Rest-pause: At failure, rest about 15 seconds, then go to failure again.
glossary.Stretched half reps (lengthened partials: After failure, keep doing half reps in the stretched half of the movement.
glossary.Mechanical drop: At failure, switch straight to an easier version of the same movement and continue.
glossary.Superset (A1/A2): Alternate the paired exercises, resting as listed between them.
glossary.Ramp-up sets: Progressively heavier warm-up sets of a few reps that build to your working weight. Never to failure.

programmes.name: Relentless PPL
programmes.hook: A six-day push, pull, legs split with two different versions of every session, built to grow everything twice a week.
programmes.description: For intermediate lifters with at least a year of consistent training who can get to the gym six days a week. Each muscle is hit twice a week from two angles: the A sessions lean on stretch-focused presses and pulls for upper chest, lats and quads, the B sessions on heavy flat pressing, back thickness and the hamstrings and glutes. Main lifts stay heavy and clean, machines and cables carry the hard sets to failure, so you get plenty of growth stimulus without beating up your joints.
programmes.effort_style: Barbell presses, rows, pull-ups and RDLs stop at the last perfect rep. Machines, cables and isolation exercises go to genuine failure on every working set, with one intensity technique on the final set where listed.

programmes.progression: Double progression. Each exercise has a rep range. When you hit the top of the range on every working set, add the smallest load jump next session (2.5 kg on barbells and machines, 1 to 2 kg per dumbbell) and build the reps back up. On isolation work, add reps first and load second. If you miss the bottom of the range, keep the weight and beat it next time.
programmes.deload: The final week is a deload: same sessions and exercises, half the sets, the same weights or 10% lighter, and every set stops with 3 or more reps left. No intensity techniques. Take an early deload if your main lifts go backwards two sessions in a row, sleep and motivation drop, or joints start to ache.
programmes.why: Hitting each muscle twice a week with about 12 to 18 hard sets sits in the zone where the Pelland et al. (2024) meta-regression shows growth still climbing before returns flatten. Isolation choices favour long muscle lengths, such as seated leg curls (Maeo et al. 2021), overhead triceps work (Maeo et al. 2023) and incline curls, because training muscles in a stretched position produces more growth. Failure is saved for machines and cables, where it is safe and repeatable, while barbell lifts stay crisp so fatigue does not leak into the next session.

programmes.name: Hybrid Five
programmes.hook: Heavy upper and lower days followed by a high-output push, pull and legs block. Five days, strength and size in one week.
programmes.description: For intermediate lifters who want to get stronger on the big lifts while still training like a bodybuilder. The first two days are lower-rep strength sessions built around the bench, squat, pull-up and RDL. After a rest day, push, pull and legs switch to moderate weights, higher reps and intensity techniques. Every muscle is trained twice a week with a different rep range each time, so you get the strength of a heavy day and the volume of a pump day without either one crowding out the other.

programmes.name: Blueprint Upper/Lower
programmes.hook: Four days a week, every muscle twice, every session with a clear job. The split most lifters should run for years.
programmes.description: For lifters with six months or more of training who want a schedule that fits around work and still builds serious muscle. Upper 1 is built around horizontal pressing and rowing, Upper 2 around vertical pulling and overhead pressing. Lower 1 is squat-led, Lower 2 is hinge-led. Rest days fall naturally between pairs, so recovery is rarely a problem.

programmes.progression: Beat the logbook. Every working set should add a rep or a small amount of weight compared with last week. When you reach the top of the rep range, add load. If you fail to beat the log on an exercise two sessions running, swap it for a close variation; if you stall on several, take an extra rest day that week.

programmes.why: Growth tracks how close sets come to failure (Robinson et al. 2024), so a single genuinely all-out set captures much of the stimulus a multi-set approach provides. More sets still produce more growth on average (Pelland et al. 2024), so this programme trades some potential size for short sessions and big recovery margins. Pre-fatigue isolation work and stretch-focused exercise choices make every working set count.

programmes.progression: Double progression. Each exercise has a rep range. When you hit the top of the range on every working set, add the smallest load jump next session (2.5 kg on barbells and machines, 1 to 2 kg per dumbbell) and build the reps back up. On isolation work, add reps first and load second. If you miss the bottom of the range, keep the weight and beat it next time. Track the Priority Day most closely: it should improve every week.
programmes.deload: The final week is a deload: same sessions and exercises, half the sets, the same weights or 10% lighter, and every set stops with 3 or more reps left. No intensity techniques. Take an early deload if your main lifts go backwards two sessions in a row, sleep and motivation drop, or joints start to ache.
programmes.why: Exercises done early in a session, when you are fresh, get more reps and better performance, so lagging muscles go first on their own day after a rest day. Side delts get almost no work from pressing, so they need direct volume spread across four days to grow. The other muscles stay at a solid working volume so the extra priority work does not cost you size elsewhere.

programmes.progression: Variation ladder. When you hit the top of the rep range on every set, move to the next harder version or add weight in a backpack, then build the reps back up. Examples: push-up to deficit push-up to archer push-up; band-assisted pull-up to pull-up to weighted pull-up; box pistol to lower box to full pistol.
programmes.deload: The final week is a deload: same sessions and exercises, half the sets, the same weights or 10% lighter, and every set stops with 3 or more reps left. No intensity techniques. Take an early deload if your main lifts go backwards two sessions in a row, sleep and motivation drop, or joints start to ache.
programmes.why: Push-ups build chest and triceps as well as the bench press when effort and load are matched (Kikuchi and Nakazato 2017), and light loads grow muscle when taken close to failure. The variation ladder is how bodyweight training applies progressive overload. Exercises like Nordic curls, sissy squats and deficit push-ups load muscles in deep stretch, which tends to produce more growth.
